This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$, and for each $n\in A$ choose some $X_n\subseteq \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$. Let\[B = \{ m\in \mathbb{N} : m\not\in X_n\pmod{n}\textrm{ for all }n\in A\textrm{ with }m>n\}.\]Must $B$ have a logarithmic density, i.e. is it true that\[\lim_{x\to \infty} \frac{1}{\log x}\sum_{\substack{m\in B\\ m<x}}\frac{1}{m}\]exists?
#486: [Er61,p.235][Er80,p.114]
number theory | 
primitive sets
Davenport and Erdős [DaEr36] proved that the answer is yes when $X_n=\{0\}$ for all $n\in A$. An alternative elementary proof was later given by Davenport and Erdős in [DaEr51].
Erdős [Er80] wrote 'perhaps this question is not very difficult as far as I know it has not been attacked really seriously'.
The problem considers logarithmic density since Besicovitch [Be34] showed examples exist without a natural density, even when $X_n=\{0\}$ for all $n\in A$. 
This is a generalisation of [25] (which is the case when $\lvert X_n\rvert=1$ for all $n\in A$).
Additional thanks to: Wouter van Doorn, Leeham, and Terence Tao

 On inspection of [Er61, p.236] there is indeed an "activation threshold" condition ($b \geq a_i$ in (I.26.1) of that paper, or one should replace "$m \notin X_n \pmod{n}$" with "$m<n$ or $m \notin X_n \pmod{n}$" in the current formulation) that is currently absent, and as GPT-5.2 claims, without this condition one can easily create sparse congruence conditions that occasionally disrupt the logarithmic density and provide a cheap negative answer to the question as currently stated.
EDIT: As a side note, I am glad that the discussion of AI-generated solutions on this site is maturing from just focusing on whether an Erdos problem as literally stated on this web site was solved by the AI tool, to also addressing more holistic questions of whether the statement proven was actually in the spirit of what Erdos was intending, and what the natural variants of that statement are and how they connect with the rest of the literature. (In particular I hope we resist efforts to "benchmax" the number of solved problems on this site at the expense of understanding the broader context of these problems.)

 Some not so very deep thoughts: first, if this is true for a collection of sets $X_n$, then it is also true for the collection of their complements. Second, for finite sets $A = \{a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_k\}$, this reduces to the case $|A| = 1$ with the single element in $A$ taken to be the least common multiple of the $a_i$. In this case $B$ even has a natural density. Third, since it is known for $X_n = \{0\}$, it is also true for $X_n = \{c\}$ for any $c \in \mathbb{N}$. Finally, the logical next step would be to consider what happens if $|X_n| = 1$ for all $n$ and $X_n \subset X$ for some finite set $X$. Perhaps this isn't too difficult either.

A full proof 
claimed by Shouqiao Wang (using GPT-5.6 Sol).
 Summary:
 The answer is no: the logarithmic density does not always exist.
The idea is to add groups of congruence conditions at larger and larger scales. When a group first becomes active, it removes enough integers to push the logarithmic average down. But in the long run, the residue classes used by that group cover only a very small proportion of the integers.
We place many groups close together to make the average fall, and then leave a very long gap so that the average can rise again, while the later groups are still inactive. Repeating this gives one fixed construction in which the logarithmic average keeps moving between two different levels, so it does not converge.
 Notes:
 This proposed solution was found through my AI pipeline and was generated almost entirely by GPT-5.6 Sol. I have personally read and checked the proof, and I believe it is correct.
